title: Philosophy of Humor (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, substantive revision 2024)
key_findings: Three classic theories: superiority (Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes), relief (Shaftesbury, Spencer, Freud), incongruity (Beattie, Kant, Schopenhauer); incongruity is dominant in philosophy and psychology today.
Superiority is neither necessary nor sufficient (Hutcheson): people laugh at wordplay and their own mistakes without feeling superior.
Relief theory's hydraulic 'nervous energy' model is outdated; few scholars defend it.
Incongruity alone is not sufficient: violated expectations can also produce fear, disgust or anger; refinements add resolution (Shultz, Suls) and enjoyment of incongruity (Clark, Martin).
Author proposes humour as play; laughter as a play signal derived from the primate relaxed open-mouth display.
Ethics: humour is objectionable when it treats as a joke something that should be taken seriously; stereotype jokes keep stereotypes in circulation.
practical_applications: Use incongruity + a safe 'play frame' as the base model for wholesome jokes.
Treat superiority/aggression as a risk lever, not a default.
limitations: Philosophical overview, not empirical; final ~1% of page not read.

title: Benign Violations: Making Immoral Behavior Funny
key_findings: Psychological Science 21(8):1141-1149. Five experiments: benign moral violations elicit laughter/amusement in addition to disgust.
Three conditions make a violation benign: an alternative norm that makes it acceptable, weak commitment to the violated norm, psychological distance.
Perceiving the behaviour as both wrong and not wrong partially mediated displays of amusement (Study 2, Sobel t = 2.1).

Examples: harmless vs harmful version of the same disgusting act - amused 61% vs 28% (Study 3, N=36); church raffling a Hummer - non-churchgoers amused 92% vs churchgoers 62% (Study 4, N=39 in that comparison).
practical_applications: Joke check: is there a violation? is it clearly benign for THIS audience?
Lower commitment/raise distance (fictional characters, small stakes) to keep a joke benign.
limitations: Small US student samples (N = 36-80 per study), self-reported amusement or coded smiles; written by the theory's proponents.

title: Differentiating What Is Humorous From What Is Not
key_findings: JPSP 110(3):407-430 (online Dec 2015). Incongruity is defined in at least 4 ways in the literature: surprise, juxtaposition, atypicality, violation - and none alone separates humorous from non-humorous experiences well.

Six studies (entertainment, consumer products, social interaction): a benign violation - something that threatens well-being, identity or normative beliefs but simultaneously seems okay - differentiates humorous from non-humorous experiences better than common incongruity conceptualisations.
Main gain: fewer false predictions that joyous, amazing or tragic situations would be funny.
practical_applications: Incongruity alone can just confuse; add a 'mild threat that is OK' for laughs.
limitations: Authored by the theory's proponents; mostly US online/student samples.

title: Too Close for Comfort, or Too Far to Care? Finding Humor in Distant Tragedies and Close Mishaps
authors: A. Peter McGraw, Caleb Warren, Lawrence E. Williams, Bridget Leonard
key_findings: Psychological Science (OnlineFirst 31 Aug 2012). Five studies: tragedies (severe violations) are funnier when temporally, socially, hypothetically or spatially distant; mishaps (mild violations) are funnier when psychologically close.
Study 2 (N=87): 99% said being hit by a car would be funnier if it happened 5 years ago than yesterday; only 18% said so for stubbing a toe.
Interpretation: distance reduces threat for tragedies; closeness keeps some threat for mishaps.
practical_applications: Small everyday mishaps (spilled coffee, lost glasses) can be joked about up close; real suffering needs distance or no joke.
limitations: Mostly US MTurk/student samples; hypothetical or recalled events.
The 'rise then fall over time' (comedic sweet spot) finding is NOT in this paper - it is McGrawWilliamsWarren2014 (Hurricane Sandy). Corrected 2026-11-25.

title: Are Benign Violations Necessary for Humor? (commentary/extension)
key_findings: As summarized in search results: BVT is one of few models claiming necessary and sufficient conditions; the necessity question is treated as open; results suggest BVT can extend beyond moral content.
practical_applications: Treat BVT as a useful checklist, not a proven law.
limitations: Only a search snippet seen; publication venue and year unconfirmed.

title: You Must Be Joking! Benign Violations, Power Asymmetry, and Humor in a Broader Social Context
key_findings: As summarized in search results: some jokes whose violations are not seen as benign are still found funny; BVT does not explain why people disagree about whether something is funny; argues for power asymmetry and social context.
practical_applications: Who is joking about whom matters: a shop joking about customers is not the same as a customer joking about themself.
limitations: Full text blocked by captcha; content from search snippet; author first names and year from listing, not confirmed.

title: A two-stage model for the appreciation of jokes and cartoons: an information-processing analysis
key_findings: In Goldstein & McGhee (eds.) The Psychology of Humor. Stage 1: the ending does not follow from the setup (incongruity); stage 2: the listener finds a cognitive rule that makes the ending fit (resolution).
Became the standard reference for cognitive/neuro humour studies (per Encyclopedia of Humor Studies summary).
practical_applications: Every joke needs a findable rule: the audience must be able to 'get it' within the medium's time.
limitations: Bibliographic + encyclopedia summary only; resolution need not remove incongruity fully (Ritchie).

title: Variants of Incongruity Resolution
key_findings: Snippet: traditional incongruity-resolution is highly sequential and typically assumes full resolution; Suls and Shultz were highly influential.
practical_applications: Allow partial resolution (absurd humour) but know it is riskier for broad audiences.
limitations: Search snippet only.

title: Individual differences in uses of humor and their relation to psychological well-being: Development of the Humor Styles Questionnaire
authors: Rod A. Martin, Patricia Puhlik-Doris, Gwen Larsen, Jeanette Gray, Kelly Weir
key_findings: Journal of Research in Personality 37:48-75. HSQ: 32 items, 7-point scale, four styles: affiliative, self-enhancing (adaptive), aggressive, self-defeating (maladaptive).
Adaptive styles relate to extraversion, openness, self-esteem; maladaptive to aggression and neuroticism (secondary summary).
practical_applications: Give wholesome characters affiliative + self-enhancing humour; avoid self-defeating as a running gag for a lead.
limitations: Read via test-bank listing and secondary summaries; translated versions show reliability issues.

title: The Psychology of Humor: An Integrative Approach (2nd ed.)
authors: Rod A. Martin, Thomas E. Ford
key_findings: Standard textbook: definitions and theories, cognition, personality, physiology, social functions, development, health, applications in therapy/education/work.
practical_applications: Reference text for future deep-dives (not read this session).
limitations: Publisher page only.

title: Cultural Differences in Humor Perception, Usage, and Implications
authors: Tonglin Jiang, Hao Li, Yubo Hou
key_findings: Westerners treat humour as a desirable trait; Easterners (mostly Chinese samples) are more ambivalent, partly via Confucian devaluation.
Easterners use humour less for coping (Chinese, Japanese, Singaporean students); reportedly less aggressive and more affiliative humour, depending on collectivism/harmony.
Adaptive vs maladaptive HSQ pattern holds East and West but strength varies.
Thailand not covered; most Eastern data are Chinese samples; mainly correlational surveys.
practical_applications: For Thai/Asian audiences favour affiliative, harmony-keeping humour; be careful with aggressive teasing in brand voice.
limitations: Does not include Thailand; generalising East Asia to Thailand is DERIVED.

title: The evolution and functions of laughter and humor: a synthetic approach
key_findings: Quarterly Review of Biology 80(4):395-430. Distinguishes Duchenne (spontaneous, stimulus-driven) from non-Duchenne (volitional, strategic) laughter.
Duchenne laughter hypothesised as a medium for playful emotional contagion; non-Duchenne co-opted for many functions incl. derision and embarrassment.
practical_applications: In TTS/animation, a warm genuine laugh and a polite social laugh are different acts; direct them separately.
limitations: Evolutionary hypotheses; abstract-level reading.

title: Prosodic markers of saliency in humorous narratives
authors: Lucy Pickering, Salvatore Attardo, et al.
key_findings: Acoustic measures: punchlines are not louder than preceding text, are delivered at lower pitch and more slowly, often with laughing/smiling voice, and are NOT preceded by significant pauses.
Folk belief 'it's all about the pause' was untested before and largely unsupported for told narratives.
practical_applications: For TTS punchlines: slightly lower and slower, smile in the voice; do not insert a long dramatic pause by default.
limitations: Author list from listing; small corpora of narrated jokes; abstract-level.

title: Prosodic/multimodal markers of humor in conversation (Attardo, Pickering & Baker 2011; Attardo, Pickering, Lomotey & Menjo 2013)
authors: Salvatore Attardo, Lucy Pickering, et al.
key_findings: As summarized in search results: in conversation, humorous turns show no higher pitch, volume or speed and no significant pauses; smiling/laughter accompany humour.
2013 dyadic study: lower-pitch punchline effect did NOT replicate; smiling seems to set up the humorous frame before the joke.
practical_applications: Signal the play frame early (smile voice, playful face) rather than relying on a pause before the line.
limitations: Two papers merged under one key; exact titles/venues not confirmed; search summary only.

title: Timing is Everything: Temporal Scaffolding of Semantic Surprise in Humor
key_findings: 828 professional Chinese stand-up performances: temporal features (pause patterns, punchline timing) outweighed semantic incongruity in predicting audience appreciation.
Proposes 'dual prediction violation': a content surprise and a rhythm break together; example of a ~1.5 s pause before a distant punchline.
practical_applications: In performed/edited comedy, establish a rhythm then break it on the punch; contrasts with conversation findings above.
limitations: Conference paper (CogSci 2026), search summary only; stand-up genre, Chinese language.

title: A meta-analysis of humor in advertising
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 369 correlations: humour enhances attitude toward the ad, attention and positive affect, and purchase intention; it reduces source credibility; no evidence it raises liking of the advertiser. Also raises brand attitude (ABR).
practical_applications: Use humour for stopping power and liking; never as the vehicle for medical/expert credibility claims.
limitations: Abstract-level; effect sizes not read; mostly Western ad studies.
Spot-check 2026-11-25: "liking" narrowed to attitude toward the ad (no effect on liking of the advertiser).
Spot-check U3 2026-11-25 applied.

title: How humor in advertising works: A meta-analytic test of alternative models
key_findings: Marketing Letters 22(2):115-132. Tests how earlier explanations of humour effects may be integrated (findings not read).
practical_applications: Pending: read to know whether humour works via affect transfer or via cognition.
limitations: Bibliographic only.

title: The Impact of Humor in Advertising: A Review
authors: Marc G. Weinberger, Charles S. Gulas
key_findings: Journal of Advertising 21(4):35-59. Humour does not guarantee better ads; effect depends on objectives, audience, situation and humour type.
Cited later as: humour attracts attention and raises likability but does not reliably improve comprehension or persuasion.
practical_applications: Decide the job first (attention? liking? understanding?) before adding a joke.
limitations: Abstract + secondary citation; 2019 update by the same authors not read.

title: Humor and cultural values in print advertising: a cross-cultural study
authors: Leonidas Hatzithomas, Yorgos Zotos, Christina Boutsouki
key_findings: 12,351 UK and Greek magazine ads (3,828 humorous). Higher uncertainty-avoidance Greece leaned to informative humour.
Suggests individualistic/low-UA audiences prefer humour-dominant messages; collectivistic/high-UA audiences use humour as a vehicle for required information.
practical_applications: For Thai (collectivist, Hofstede-high UA) audiences, DERIVED: let humour carry the information rather than replace it.
limitations: Content analysis of ad supply, not audience response; Thailand not studied; search summary.

title: CDC's Use of Social Media and Humor in a Risk Campaign — 'Preparedness 101: Zombie Apocalypse'
key_findings: Journal of Applied Communication Research 43(2):222-241. Campaign met reach goals, but in the experiment students shown the comical zombie version reported weaker intentions to take protective action; authors: a light tone can trivialise perceived importance.
practical_applications: Health-related calls to action (eye exams, UV protection) should not be wrapped in a joke that makes the risk feel unreal.
limitations: Student sample; search summary; other studies (e.g. measles/MMR humour) found humour reduced reactance — mixed field.

title: Lessons learned: match your humor to your message
authors: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Health Communication
key_findings: Harvard Chan Center for Health Communication 'Lessons Learned' (3 Sep 2024) summarising a Health Communication study (DOI 10.1080/10410236.2023.2218532): 882 participants saw COVID memes paired with prevention- or promotion-focused messages.
Prevention messages (avoid a bad behaviour) were shared/engaged with more when paired with inoffensive humour that points out something unexpected.
Promotion messages (adopt a good behaviour) were shared more with AGGRESSIVE humour that makes fun of people who don't adopt the behaviour - explained by psychological-distance 'fit'.
Outcome = self-reported intention to share/engage, not behaviour change.
practical_applications: Use gentle surprise humour, not mockery, around health topics.
limitations: Institutional blog summarising one study; original paper not read. Earlier entry wrongly said 'playful > aggressive' - corrected 2026-11-25.

title: Effects of humor on sentence memory
key_findings: JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. Humorous sentences better remembered than non-humorous versions in free and cued recall.
Later work: advantage appears in mixed lists, not pure lists (distinctiveness); Schmidt & Williams 2001 argued against pure distinctiveness/rehearsal — mechanism contested.
practical_applications: One funny slide among plain ones is memorable; a whole feed of jokes loses the advantage (DERIVED from mixed-list finding).
limitations: Search summary; lab sentences, not ads.

title: A Computational Model of Linguistic Humor in Puns
key_findings: Cognitive Science 40(5):1270-1285. Two information-theoretic measures from a noisy-channel model of sentence processing: ambiguity (both meanings active) and distinctiveness (each meaning supported by different words).

435 sentences (phonetic puns with identical or near homophones, plus matched non-puns, from 'Pun of the Day'); funniness rated by MTurk participants (100 raters for the 195 identical-homophone sentences).
Both measures correlate with funniness; ambiguity separates puns from non-puns, distinctiveness separates exceptionally funny puns from mediocre ones.
practical_applications: A good pun needs BOTH meanings supported by different words in the line; Thai homophone puns can be checked the same way (DERIVED).
limitations: English homophone puns only; read via Europe PMC full-text XML.

title: Spoonerism: a Creative Way of Communication in Thai
key_findings: Search summary: Thai spoonerism (คำผวน) is both a speech error and intentional wordplay; used for taboo avoidance in polite register; describes the 'Luu' secret spoonerist language (often gossipy, impolite casual talk).
practical_applications: คำผวน is a native Thai humour device, but swaps often surface hidden rude/sexual readings — every คำผวน must be checked in both directions.
limitations: Conference paper; PDF returned 403; only search summary.

title: สุนทรียะคำผวน: เพศ พฤติกรรมการสมสู่ การสร้างคำใหม่และการสื่อสาร (Aesthetic of Spoonerism: Sex, Behavior of Sexual Intercourse, Word Formation and Communication)
authors: Mallika Phumathon (มัลลิกา ภูมะธน), Dirak Duangloy (ดิเรก ด้วงลอย), Nakhon Sawan Rajabhat University
key_findings: Journal of Interdisciplinary Innovation Review 4(2), Jul-Dec 2021 (TCI). Academic article built from documents, prior research and conversations with colleagues skilled at คำผวน - not an empirical study.

Summarised functions of คำผวน: (1) creates new words, (2) a communication tool, (3) a linguistic trick, (4) avoids impolite words / makes them polite, (5) creates humour and language entertainment; methods: swapping vowels and final consonants, multi-syllable swaps, selective tone shifts.

Discusses classical examples (e.g. Sunthorn Phu) and the large share of คำผวน that resolve to sexual meanings; the author notes that frequent sexual spoonerisms at work start to feel excessive ('ผวนจนเกินงาม').
practical_applications: Confirms that sexual double meaning is a central register of คำผวน — red line for a wholesome brand.
limitations: Essay-style academic article with personal observation; no audience data.

title: An Analysis of Linguistic Humor in the Humorous Scenes of Pee Mak Phra Kanong
key_findings: Trends of Humanities and Social Sciences Research 7(2):106-124 (Univ. of Phayao). Pee Mak Phra Kanong has 76 humorous scenes (identified by the producers, GDH); every fifth scene was analysed - 15 scenes, 16 humour instances.
Techniques (Berger 1997 + Pinit-Phuwadol 1998): analogy 4 (25%), pun 3 (18.75%), loanwords 3 (18.75%); ridicule, slang, explanation, mispronunciation, facetiousness, over-literalness 1 each (6.25%).
Analogy worked best combined with pun and exaggeration; slang, explanation and mispronunciation are outside Berger's taxonomy but drew laughs - Thai-specific categories needed.

Spoonerism appears only in the literature review (as phonological deviation); it was not among the techniques found in the sampled scenes. Most humour came from conversations of the added supporting characters.
practical_applications: Thai mainstream comedy leans on wordplay and analogy — fits Mint & Tao dialogue.
limitations: One film, 15 scenes, analysis of the producers' intended humour - not audience response.

title: A Linguistic Strategies to Express Humor in Thai Context
key_findings: International Journal of Social Science and Humanity 6(6), June 2016. Data: five Thai situation comedies; frameworks: speech acts, Grice's cooperative principle, implicature.
Six categories of humour-related speech acts: boasting, expressing condescension, threatening, blaming, teasing and satire.
Humour in Thai sitcoms is closely associated with superiority and aggression created by the speaker; humour also arises from non-observance of Gricean maxims (violating or flouting).
practical_applications: Mainstream Thai sitcom humour is often put-down based; a wholesome brand should consciously NOT copy that default.
limitations: Qualitative analysis of scripted TV; no audience measure; 4-page conference-style paper.

title: (Laughter in American English and Central Thai television talk)
key_findings: Search summary: laughter use varies cross-linguistically between American English and Central Thai TV, aligning with linguistic patterns and cultural values.
practical_applications: Thai laughter placement in VO should follow Thai norms, not dubbed-English habits.
limitations: Title not confirmed; snippet only.

title: Pie and Chase: Gag, Spectacle and Narrative in Slapstick Comedy
key_findings: Search summary: frames slapstick as a tension between the gag (spectacle, 'pie') and narrative ('chase'); rethinks the gag's role in classical comic film.
practical_applications: Physical gags in clips should either push the story or be a deliberate pause from it — know which.
limitations: Snippet and blog summary only; open-access chapter not read.

title: The comedy rule of 3s (blog post)
key_findings: Ken Levine blog (16 Jul 2017): the rule of three (comic triple) establishes a pattern and ends with something unexpected ('We serve lasagna, spaghetti, and poi').
Two items are usually enough to set the pattern; more than three feels wrong.
Traps: the first two items must clearly establish the pattern; keep setups straight (a funny setup cancels the payoff); don't make setups convoluted.
practical_applications: Template for 3-slide carousel jokes.
limitations: Craft, tier D. Callbacks and A/B-plot structure are NOT in this post (other practitioner pages).

title: What Makes Things Funny? An Integrative Review of the Antecedents of Laughter and Amusement
authors: Caleb Warren, Adam Barsky, A. Peter McGraw
key_findings: Personality and Social Psychology Review 25(1):41-65. More than 20 psychological humour theories draw on five candidate antecedents: surprise, simultaneity, superiority, a violation appraisal, and conditions for a benign appraisal.
Against the evidence, simultaneity, violation and benign appraisals help distinguish humorous from non-humorous experiences; surprise and superiority do not.

Surprise is too broad (muggings, diagnoses surprise without amusement) and too narrow: expected punchlines were rated funnier (Kenny 1955; Pollio & Mers 1974), partial prior exposure made jokes funnier (Topolinski 2014), rewatch enjoyment equals first viewing (O'Brien 2019); callbacks and running gags work.
When surprise and violation were manipulated orthogonally (candy offered vs thrown, warned vs not), violations increased laughter; surprise did not.
Failed attempts at humour make people/organisations seem incompetent or insensitive and can elicit disgust, anger and disapproval.
practical_applications: Don't chase 'surprise' as the core of a joke: build two simultaneous readings + a small violation + a clear 'it's okay' signal.
Running gags and callbacks are evidence-compatible; a known punchline can still land if it is a benign violation.
limitations: Written by BVT proponents; integrative (not systematic) review; underlying studies mostly Western students.

title: The Rise and Fall of Humor: Psychological Distance Modulates Humorous Responses to Tragedy
authors: A. Peter McGraw, Lawrence E. Williams, Caleb Warren
key_findings: Social Psychological and Personality Science 5(5), starting p. 566 (online Dec 2013). Longitudinal: about 100 different participants at each of 10 time points rated three Hurricane Sandy joke tweets (from one day before landfall to 99 days after).

Humour fell as the reality set in (day -1 M = 3.5 to day 8 M = 2.9), was lowest at day 15 (M = 2.7, 'too soon'), peaked at day 36 (M = 3.4), and fell again by day 99 (M = 2.6) - a comedic sweet spot, not a monotonic rise with time.
Changes in humour were mediated by perceived offensiveness (threat).
practical_applications: Topical jokes about a bad event have a window: not while it is fresh, and not once it no longer matters to the audience.
limitations: One US event, online samples, three tweets; 7-point ratings.
